title: Early Dynastic Period of Egypt
capsule: The Early Dynastic Period of Egypt, spanning the First and Second Dynasties (c. 3100–2686 BC), immediately followed the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt, traditionally attributed to Narmer (often equated with the legendary Menes), whose Palette records the conquest of the Delta around 3100 BC. The capital was established at Thinis, then shifted to the newly founded Memphis, which would remain Egypt's administrative center for millennia. During this period the essential institutions of pharaonic civilization were consolidated: divine kingship, hieroglyphic writing, monumental mud-brick mastaba tombs, and the administrative machinery of a territorial state. The period ended with Khasekhemwy, last ruler of the Second Dynasty, whose reign saw the unification of residual factional conflicts and set the stage for the Old Kingdom pyramid age.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Nile Valley core is well-defined archaeologically, but Egyptian control over the Sinai and southern Canaan during this period was episodic and the outer frontier is contested; the geometric attestation window (-3000 to -2500) is a reasonable approximation given the uncertainties of pre-2700 BC Egyptian chronology.
